spans.text: VA disability compensation is monthly, tax-free pay from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs to veterans with a physical or mental condition connected to military service. This page explains how the program is structured in 2026: pay rates effective December 1, 2025, how the rating system works, how to file or appeal, and where to get free accredited help. Every figure below links to its official source on VA.gov, Benefits.va.gov, or the eCFR.

The VA rates each service-connected condition from 0% to 100% in 10% increments using the Schedule for Rating Disabilities (

Each diagnostic code has its own criteria. The VA assigns the rating based on the evidence in the claims file — typically service treatment records, private and VA medical records, lay statements, and the Compensation & Pension (C&P) exam.
When a veteran has multiple conditions, the VA combines them using the table at
— not simple addition. Each rating reduces the "remaining efficiency" of a hypothetical healthy person, and the result is rounded to the nearest 10%.
A 50% rating combined with another 50% rating yields 75% under §4.25 (50% takes half of the remaining 50%), which rounds to 80%. Two 50% conditions do not combine to 100%.

blocks.question: Is VA disability permanent?

spans.text: Not automatically. The VA can propose a reduction if it finds the condition has improved. Continuous ratings receive additional protection at 5, 10, and 20 years under 38 CFR §3.951 and §3.957. A "Permanent and Total" designation removes scheduled re-exams. Confirm your status on VA.gov.

blocks.question: Is VA disability taxable?

spans.text: No. VA disability compensation is exempt from federal income tax per the IRS. Most states also exempt it, but state treatment varies — check your state tax authority.

blocks.question: Can I work and collect VA disability?

spans.text: A veteran rated at 100% schedular may continue to work. Total Disability based on Individual Unemployability (TDIU) has earnings limits tied to substantially gainful employment. See VA.gov for the current rules.

blocks.question: How long do VA claims take?

spans.text: VA publishes live timeliness data on VA.gov. Recent averages have been roughly 4–5 months for an initial decision; Board of Veterans' Appeals decisions can take 12–24 months or longer. Check the current average on VA.gov before relying on a specific number.

blocks.question: Can my rating be reduced?

spans.text: Before the 20-year protection mark, yes — the VA can schedule re-examinations if it has reason to believe the condition has improved. Ratings held continuously for 20+ years and ratings designated Permanent and Total receive additional protection.

blocks.question: What's the difference between VA disability and SSDI?

spans.text: VA disability is service-connected compensation paid by the VA with no income limit. SSDI is paid by the Social Security Administration for a disability that prevents substantial work, regardless of cause, and has SSA-defined earnings limits. The two programs are independent and many veterans receive both.

blocks.question: Do I need a lawyer to file a claim?

spans.text: For an initial claim, no. An accredited Veterans Service Organization (VSO) can file the claim at no cost. For appeals after a denial, an accredited attorney or claims agent may charge a fee under VA rules (38 CFR §14.636). Verify accreditation in the VA Office of General Counsel database.

spans.text: Veterans Day is the United States' annual tribute to everyone who has worn the uniform of the U.S. armed forces. In 2026 it falls on Wednesday, November 11 — the same date every year, chosen to mark the moment the guns fell silent at the end of World War I. This page explains where the holiday comes from, how it differs from Memorial Day and Armed Forces Day, how the U.S. Navy marks the day, and concrete ways to honor the veterans in your community.

NavyWeek.org is independent and not affiliated with the U.S. Navy, NAVCO, or the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. Dates and program details are summarized from official sources linked throughout this page.

items.label: Veterans Day vs. Memorial Day vs. Armed Forces Day

spans.text: Veterans Day is a U.S. federal holiday held on November 11 each year to honor everyone who has served in the United States armed forces — the Navy, Marine Corps, Army, Air Force, Space Force, and Coast Guard — whether in war or peacetime, and whether they are living or have passed away (

Unlike many federal holidays that move to a Monday, Veterans Day stays anchored to November 11. The date itself is the point: it commemorates the armistice that ended the fighting of World War I at 11:00 a.m. on November 11, 1918.
The federal government writes it as "Veterans Day" — no apostrophe. It is a day for honoring all veterans, not a day that belongs to them, so the possessive apostrophe is intentionally omitted.
. President Woodrow Wilson first proclaimed November 11, 1919, to commemorate the first anniversary of the end of World War I (

In 1938, Congress made November 11 a legal federal holiday "dedicated to the cause of world peace and to be hereafter celebrated and known as 'Armistice Day.'" After World War II and the Korean War, veterans service organizations urged Congress to broaden the day to honor all American veterans. In
, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed legislation changing the name from Armistice Day to

For a few years the date moved: the Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 shifted Veterans Day to the fourth Monday in October beginning in 1971. The change proved unpopular — many states kept observing November 11 — and in 1975 President Gerald Ford signed a law returning Veterans Day to its original November 11 date, effective 1978, where it has remained ever since.

blocks.text: VETERANS DAY VS. MEMORIAL DAY VS. ARMED FORCES DAY

spans.text: These three observances are often confused. Each honors a different group:
Memorial Day remembers the fallen; Veterans Day thanks all who served; Armed Forces Day recognizes those serving right now.

blocks.text: HOW THE U.S. NAVY OBSERVES VETERANS DAY

spans.text: Across the fleet, the Navy marks Veterans Day with ceremonies at bases, aboard ships, and in communities. Typical observances include wreath-layings at memorials, color guard presentations, moments of silence, and Navy band performances. Current Sailors frequently join veterans at local parades and ceremonies (

Most communities hold a Veterans Day observance — many on or near November 11. Local VFW and American Legion posts are good places to find one.
A simple, sincere acknowledgment of a veteran's service is meaningful — at work, in your family, or in your neighborhood.

blocks.question: When is Veterans Day 2026?

spans.text: Veterans Day 2026 is observed on Wednesday, November 11, 2026. Veterans Day is always commemorated on November 11 each year, regardless of the day of the week, because the date marks the anniversary of the 1918 Armistice that ended the fighting in World War I.

blocks.question: Why is Veterans Day on November 11?

spans.text: The fighting of World War I ended with an armistice that took effect at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month — 11:00 a.m. on November 11, 1918. The United States first marked the date as Armistice Day in 1919, Congress made it an annual observance in 1938, and in 1954 it was renamed Veterans Day to honor veterans of all American wars.

blocks.question: What's the difference between Veterans Day and Memorial Day?

spans.text: Veterans Day (November 11) honors all who have served in the U.S. armed forces — living and deceased. Memorial Day (the last Monday in May) specifically honors service members who died while serving. A simple way to remember it: Memorial Day remembers those who gave their lives; Veterans Day thanks all who served.

blocks.question: How is Veterans Day different from Armed Forces Day?

spans.text: Armed Forces Day (the third Saturday in May) honors people who are currently serving on active duty. Veterans Day honors those who have served and are no longer on active duty, while Memorial Day honors those who died in service. Together the three observances cover current members, former members, and the fallen.

blocks.question: Is Veterans Day a federal holiday?

spans.text: Yes. Veterans Day is one of the eleven U.S. federal holidays. Federal offices are generally closed, and many schools, banks, and businesses observe it as well. When November 11 falls on a weekend, federal employees typically receive the adjacent Friday or Monday as the observed day off — but the commemoration itself stays on November 11.

blocks.question: How does the U.S. Navy observe Veterans Day?

spans.text: The Navy marks Veterans Day with wreath-laying ceremonies, ship and base observances, community events, and outreach through the Navy Office of Community Outreach (NAVCO). Navy bands perform, color guards present the colors, and current Sailors join veterans at memorials and parades nationwide to recognize those who served.

blocks.question: Is there a Navy Week happening around Veterans Day 2026?

spans.text: Yes. Flagstaff Navy Week runs November 9–16, 2026 — the grand finale of the 2026 "Road Trip to 250" — and includes Veterans Day on November 11. It is a natural opportunity to connect with Sailors, attend Navy band performances, and honor veterans in person.

blocks.question: What are good ways to honor veterans on Veterans Day?

spans.text: You can attend a local Veterans Day ceremony or parade, thank a veteran in your life, fly the U.S. flag, support reputable veteran service organizations, volunteer at a VA medical center, or visit a national cemetery or memorial. Many businesses also offer recognition to veterans on the day.

blocks.question: Is Veterans Day spelled with an apostrophe?

spans.text: No. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs uses "Veterans Day" without an apostrophe. The holiday is not a day that "belongs to" veterans (possessive); it is a day for honoring all veterans (attributive), so no apostrophe is used.

spans.text: Most veterans want to stay in their own homes as they age. The trouble is that figuring out how the VA actually pays for that help can feel like its own full-time job. There are two completely different programs that both get called "veterans home care," they have separate applications, and a social worker will rarely sit you down and explain the difference.

This guide does that. By the end, you'll know which VA programs provide hands-on care, which one sends a monthly check you can use to pay for care yourself, who qualifies, and how to apply without paying anyone a fee to do it.

A bit of context on why this matters: there were about 8.1 million veterans aged 65 or older in 2021, and nearly half of all U.S. veterans are now 65 or older. The demand for in-home help is climbing fast, and the families who understand their options end up with far better care and far less out-of-pocket spending than the ones who don't.

blocks.text: THE ONE THING MOST FAMILIES GET WRONG

spans.text: Here's the distinction that trips everyone up. The VA runs two separate branches that both touch home care, and they don't talk to each other the way you'd expect.
provides or arranges actual care. A nurse, an aide, or a medical team shows up at the house. You don't get cash; you get services.
sends money. The main program here is
, a tax-free monthly pension supplement you can spend on whatever care you choose, including hiring a private agency or, in many cases, a family member.
Two branches, two applications, two sets of rules. Some families qualify for both. The rest of this guide is organized around that split, so keep it in mind as you read.
One more practical note: the VA doesn't directly employ the aides who come to your home. It contracts that work out through its
— five regional networks managed by outside administrators (Optum handles Regions 1–3; TriWest handles Regions 4–5). That's why the agency at your door is a local company, not a VA employee.

blocks.text: VA HOME CARE PROGRAMS (THE SERVICES SIDE)

spans.text: These are the VHA programs that put care in the home. You generally need to be enrolled in VA health care first (more on that below), and a VA social worker assesses what you need before any service starts. Here's what's on the menu.

blocks.text: Homemaker and Home Health Aide care

spans.text: This is the program most people picture when they say "home care." A trained aide comes to the house and helps with the daily things that have gotten hard — bathing, dressing, grooming, preparing meals, getting around safely. The aide isn't a nurse, but a registered nurse supervises the care.
It's open to enrolled veterans of any age who meet the clinical criteria and live where the service is available. Depending on your service-connected status, a copay may apply.

Don't confuse this with the aide program. HBPC sends a full VA medical team into the home — a physician or nurse practitioner, a nurse, a social worker, a dietitian, a therapist, a pharmacist, sometimes a psychologist. It's ongoing primary medical care for veterans with complex chronic conditions who have a genuinely hard time getting to a clinic.
It's part of the standard VA medical benefits package, availability depends on your location, and a copay may apply based on the financial assessment from VA Form 10-10EC.

VDC is the flexible option. Instead of the VA assigning you an agency, you get a monthly budget tied to your level of need and you hire your own workers — which can include friends, neighbors, and certain family members. An Area Agency on Aging counselor helps you set it up, and a financial management service handles the paychecks (you never touch the cash directly).
You don't need a service-connected disability rating for VDC, but it's only offered in certain locations, and budgets in practice rarely run above roughly $4,500 a month.

This is short-term, doctor-ordered medical care: wound care, catheter management, physical or occupational or speech therapy delivered at home by a community agency. It's especially useful for veterans who live outside a VA service area.

Respite exists for the caregiver, not just the veteran. It covers short-term care — in the home or in a facility — so a family caregiver can rest, travel, or handle an emergency. Eligible veterans can receive up to 30 days of respite care per year.

Hospice is for veterans facing a terminal illness who are no longer pursuing a cure; palliative care can run alongside active treatment to manage symptoms. Both are available to enrolled veterans who meet the clinical need, in any setting,
. The VA also provides bereavement support to families for 13 months afterward.

blocks.text: Adult day health care and home telehealth

spans.text: Rounding things out: adult day health care gives veterans a supervised, social daytime program (and gives caregivers a break), and home telehealth lets a care team monitor health conditions remotely. Both help families keep a veteran at home longer.

VA geriatric and extended-care services charge no copay for the first 21 days of care in any 12-month period. If a copay applies at all, it starts on day 22 and depends on your service-connected status and income. Hospice is always copay-free.

blocks.text: AID AND ATTENDANCE: THE PROGRAM THAT PAYS YOU

spans.text: Aid and Attendance (A&A) is the cash side. It's a monthly supplement added on top of the basic Veterans Pension or Survivors Pension — which means you have to qualify for that underlying pension first; A&A can't be paid on its own.
The money is tax-free and yours to direct. Most families use it to pay a home care agency or a family caregiver.

Here's the catch that the table hides: these are
. The actual payment equals the maximum annual pension rate minus your countable income, divided by 12. So if you have income, your check is smaller.

This is the part that gets families who assume they earn too much to qualify. Your unreimbursed medical expenses — including what you pay for home care — that exceed 5% of the maximum pension rate get subtracted from your countable income. For a lot of applicants, the cost of care itself is what brings their "countable" income low enough to qualify. If a quick glance at your income made you think you're over the line, don't stop there.

blocks.text: WHAT IT COSTS: VA-FUNDED CARE VS. PRIVATE PAY

spans.text: When the VA arranges care through its Community Care Network, your out-of-pocket cost is usually little or nothing (subject to the copay rules above). The tradeoff is that the VA's clinical assessment — not your family — decides the type and number of hours.

Private-pay home care is more flexible but adds up. The national median for a non-medical caregiver hit $35 per hour in the 2025 CareScout (Genworth) Cost of Care Survey — about $80,080 a year at 44 hours a week. Skilled in-home nursing runs closer to $90 an hour.
That gap is exactly where Aid and Attendance earns its keep. The monthly benefit bridges the difference between what the VA provides directly and the additional private help many families want.

blocks.text: CAN YOU PAY A FAMILY MEMBER TO PROVIDE CARE?

spans.text: Yes — and this is one of the most common questions families ask. There are three routes, and the rules differ in one important way.
The veteran or spouse receives the benefit and uses it to pay a caregiver. That caregiver can be an adult child, another relative, a friend, or a professional —
, since spousal income is already counted. Set up a written care agreement and keep clean records (the "nanny tax" rules apply).
(the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers). This one pays a monthly stipend directly to the caregiver — and here a spouse

be the paid caregiver. It also adds health coverage, mental-health support, and respite. The bar is higher: the veteran needs a VA disability rating of 70% or more and at least six months of needed personal care. Apply with VA Form 10-10CG. (A September 2025 rule extended the program's "legacy" transition period through September 30, 2028, so reassessment rules are still shifting.)
As covered above, you can hire and pay family members (other than a spouse) out of your VDC budget.

blocks.text: HOW TO CHOOSE A VETERANS HOME CARE AGENCY

spans.text: A few things separate a smooth experience from a frustrating one:
If you're using VA-arranged care, the agency must be in the Community Care Network — properly licensed or certified and in good standing.
Name your preferred provider to your VA social worker before a referral is automatically assigned.
For Aid and Attendance, you have freedom.
You can use any qualified agency or hire privately, since you're paying with your own benefit.
An agency that regularly bills the VA and handles Aid and Attendance paperwork will save you real headaches.

blocks.question: Does the VA pay for in-home care?

spans.text: Yes, in two ways: it arranges and largely covers services through its health system, and it provides the Aid and Attendance pension you can use to pay for care yourself.

blocks.question: How many hours of home care does the VA provide?

spans.text: There's no fixed national number. Hours are set by a clinical assessment of your needs, so they vary from one veteran to the next.

blocks.question: Who qualifies for VA home care?

spans.text: For service programs, enrolled veterans with an assessed clinical need. For Aid and Attendance, veterans who meet the service, status, care-need, and financial criteria described above.

blocks.question: Can I be paid to care for my veteran spouse?

spans.text: Not through Aid and Attendance — but yes through PCAFC, which can pay a spouse a monthly stipend if the veteran has a 70%+ disability rating and meets the other requirements.

blocks.question: What's the income and net worth limit for Aid and Attendance?

spans.text: The net worth limit is $163,699 for 2026. Your primary home and one vehicle are excluded.

blocks.question: How much is Aid and Attendance per month in 2026?

spans.text: Up to roughly $2,424 for a single veteran, $2,874 for a veteran with one dependent, and $1,558 for a surviving spouse — minus any countable income.

blocks.question: What's the difference between VA home care and Aid and Attendance?

spans.text: VA home care is a service the VA arranges. Aid and Attendance is cash you receive and spend on care yourself.

blocks.question: Does the VA cover hospice at home?

spans.text: Yes, with no copays, in any setting, plus 13 months of bereavement support for the family.

blocks.question: How long does an Aid and Attendance claim take?

spans.text: Usually three to six months or more, with benefits paid retroactively to your filing date.

blocks.question: Will I have a copay for VA home care?

spans.text: No copay for the first 21 days of care in a 12-month period. After that, it depends on your service-connected status and income. Hospice is always free.

blocks.question: Can a veteran with dementia get home care through the VA?

spans.text: Yes. Dementia-related needs are exactly the kind of clinical need these programs are built to assess and cover.

blocks.question: What credit cards waive the annual fee for military?

spans.text: American Express, Chase, Citi, and U.S. Bank waive annual fees on personal cards for active-duty servicemembers under both SCRA and MLA — MLA also covers military spouses on their own cards. Capital One waives fees only under SCRA, which means the account must have been opened before active duty began. Navy Federal waives its $49 Flagship fee only under SCRA. Veterans and retirees are not covered by either law.

blocks.question: Does American Express waive annual fees for military?

spans.text: Yes. American Express waives annual fees on all personal cards for active-duty servicemembers under both SCRA and MLA. MLA relief is applied automatically when an eligible servicemember or spouse opens a card during active duty; SCRA relief on pre-service accounts must be requested. Military spouses qualify for the MLA waiver on their own cards, not just as authorized users.

blocks.question: Does Chase waive credit card fees for military spouses?

spans.text: Yes. Under the Military Lending Act, spouses of active-duty servicemembers are "covered borrowers," so a spouse can open their own Chase personal card — including the Sapphire Reserve or Preferred — and have the annual fee waived. There is no requirement to be an authorized user; separate accounts also mean each spouse can earn their own welcome offer. Chase verifies MLA status automatically against the Department of Defense database.

blocks.question: What is the difference between SCRA and MLA?

spans.text: SCRA (the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act) applies to credit you opened BEFORE active duty: it caps interest at 6% on pre-service debt, counts fees as interest, and must be requested. MLA (the Military Lending Act) applies to credit you open DURING active duty: it caps the Military APR at 36%, is applied automatically, and covers spouses and dependents enrolled in DEERS. Because annual fees count toward the 36% MAPR, major issuers simply waive them on MLA-covered accounts.

blocks.question: Do veterans get SCRA or MLA credit card benefits?

spans.text: No. Both laws protect servicemembers on active duty only. SCRA relief can be requested up to 180 days after leaving active duty for debt incurred before service, but once that window closes the protections end, and MLA coverage ends when active service ends. Veterans should optimize for rewards and no-annual-fee cards instead — or credit-union programs like PenFed’s Honors Advantage, which explicitly includes honorably discharged veterans.

blocks.question: Does Capital One waive the Venture X annual fee for active duty?

spans.text: Only under SCRA — never under MLA. That means the Venture X (or any Capital One card) must have been opened before your active-duty period began; open it during active duty and you will pay the $395 fee. Capital One’s SCRA program caps interest at 4%, better than the statutory 6%, and one request covers Discover accounts too, since Discover is now part of Capital One.

blocks.question: Do military credit card fee waivers apply to National Guard and Reserve?

spans.text: Yes, while on qualifying orders. Guard and Reserve members serving on active orders of 30 or more consecutive days (Title 10, or Title 32 for SCRA-covered National Guard service) are treated as active duty for these protections, as are commissioned officers of the Public Health Service and NOAA. One practical play for Capital One cards: open the card before a qualifying activation, then request SCRA once on orders.

blocks.question: What is the maximum interest rate on a credit card for active-duty military?

spans.text: Two caps apply. Under SCRA, interest on debt you incurred before active duty is capped at 6% — and fees count as interest, with the excess forgiven, not deferred. Under MLA, credit opened during active duty is capped at a 36% Military APR (MAPR), which also counts most fees. Several issuers voluntarily beat the SCRA cap: Capital One, Navy Federal, and USAA all cap covered accounts at 4%.

blocks.question: Is the Amex Platinum worth it for military?

spans.text: For active-duty servicemembers, it is one of the strongest cards available: the $895 annual fee is waived under both SCRA and MLA, so you keep the lounge access and the card’s long menu of statement credits at no annual cost. A spouse can hold their own fee-waived Platinum under MLA. For veterans, the math changes — no waiver applies, so it is only worth it if you actually use enough of the credits and travel benefits to beat the fee.

blocks.question: What happens to my credit cards when I leave active duty?

spans.text: MLA and SCRA fee waivers end when your covered status ends, so plan for annual fees to return. In practice fees may not resume immediately — issuers periodically re-check the DoD database — but budget as if they will. Before separation, decide card by card: keep the ones whose benefits beat the fee, downgrade the rest to no-fee versions rather than canceling, and avoid closing your oldest account, which shortens your credit history.

NavyWeek publishes one thing about military and veteran discounts: what we can prove. Every figure on this site traces back to a primary source we read ourselves — and dated.
This page explains exactly how we do that, step by step, so you can judge our work — and so the people who rely on it know what stands behind it.
We treat this as a high-stakes subject. A wrong percentage sends a veteran to a counter expecting a discount that was never real. Accuracy isn't a constraint on what we do here — it is the work.

cards.title: Choose

cards.title: Compare

cards.title: Verify
cards.desc: Run each page through a publish gate it must pass to ship.

blocks.heading: How we choose what to cover

spans.text: We don't cover brands at random, and we don't cover them because an affiliate program pays well — we have no such arrangements. We maintain a research queue ranked by search demand: the brands and questions service members and veterans look up most. We deliberately also cover brands that turn out to have no military discount. That's a real, useful answer — more honest than the coupon pages that invent an offer to fill the gap.

The governing rule is simple and absolute: we never state a discount amount, eligible group, code, stacking claim, or term we haven’t confirmed against a primary source. When a source doesn’t confirm something, we say what is confirmed and flag the rest as unverified. An honest "the brand publishes no exact percentage" beats a confident, fabricated number. For every fact, we record the source URL, who owns it, the date it was updated, the date we accessed it, the exact fact, and our confidence in it.

blocks.heading: Finding the genuinely best way to save

spans.text: A page that only answers "does this brand have a military discount?" leaves money on the table — the official discount is frequently not the best deal. For each brand we compare every legitimate path against one realistic example cart: the official discount, third-party programs, cashback routes, sale-stacking, credit-card and loyalty plays, and outlet channels. The make-or-break question is stacking — what can legally be combined — verified against both the brand’s terms and the provider’s.

blocks.heading: We work sources in a fixed order of authority

rows.title: The brand's own pages
rows.desc: Discount, help, terms, checkout, or offer page. The top source for the percentage, codes, and fine print.

rows.title: The verification provider's brand page
rows.desc: ID.me, SheerID, GovX, WeSalute, VerifyPass — often states the exact percentage and eligible groups.

rows.title: Store locator, support, return policy
rows.desc: For in-store rules, regional limits, and exclusions.

rows.title: Reputable military & editorial resources
rows.desc: Context only. These go stale quickly, so we verify against the brand before publishing.

rows.title: Coupon & aggregator sites
rows.desc: Never treated as fact. We read them only to see what false claims are circulating so we can correct them. They are the problem we exist to fix.

blocks.note: The most authoritative source always wins. Anything below high confidence gets hedged in the copy — or left out entirely.

blocks.heading: A brand cannot be published unless we have all of this
blocks.lead: Research becomes a page only after it clears a gate. A documented "no discount exists" finding passes too — it meets the same standard of proof.

cards.title: A working brand link
cards.desc: A verified link to the brand's own discount page — https://, not an affiliate link, not a dead link, not a generic homepage.

cards.title: The verification mechanic
cards.desc: Which provider gates the offer, and how a customer proves eligibility.

cards.title: The discount value
cards.desc: The actual value — or an explicit, sourced statement that the brand publishes none.

cards.title: Material exclusions
cards.desc: Caps, excluded categories, one-code-per-order windows, regional limits, no-stacking rules.

blocks.heading: What we will not do
blocks.lead: To make the standard concrete — here is what we refuse to do, even when it would be easier or more profitable.
items: Publish a percentage, code, or eligibility rule we couldn't verify at the source.
Treat a coupon or aggregator site as proof of anything.
Claim an audience — reserve, Guard, retiree, spouse, dependent — the brand doesn't actually name.
Present an expired or limited promo as a standing, evergreen offer.
Imply a partnership or endorsement that doesn't exist, or let affiliate incentives decide what we say.
Emit fabricated merchant ratings, reviews, or offer markup — we are a publisher, not the seller.
